o: A system of small independent services communicating via APIs
items.e: Microservices: each service has its own codebase, deployment and scaling. They communicate over HTTP/gRPC/queues.

items.q: What is the difference between a monolith and microservices?
o: A monolith — one process, easier to develop; microservices — distributed, more complex but more scalable
A monolith is always split into many services, while microservices run as a single process
Microservices are always simpler than a monolith since they have no network, contracts or separate deploys
A monolith and microservices are architecturally the same, only repository names differ
items.e: Monolith: easy to develop, hard to scale partially. Microservices: independent deploys, but harder testing and debugging.

o: A single entry point for all clients that routes requests to microservices
items.e: API Gateway: authentication, rate limiting, routing, SSL termination, logging — in one place in front of all services.

o: Distributes incoming requests across multiple servers for even load
items.e: Load Balancer: Round Robin, Least Connections, IP Hash — algorithms. Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB — examples. Horizontal scaling.

items.q: What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
o: A network of distributed servers delivering static content from the node closest to the user
A message delivery queue between services with ordering guarantees and retries
A distributed database accepting writes on edge nodes and replacing the origin server
A network of microservices where each service is deployed closer to the user for business logic
items.e: A CDN caches static assets (JS, CSS, images) on edge servers worldwide. Reduces latency and origin server load.

items.q: What is horizontal vs vertical scaling?
o: Horizontal — more instances; vertical — more resources on one server
items.e: Scale out (horizontal): add servers — unlimited but more complex. Scale up (vertical): more CPU/RAM — simple but capped.

o: REST — HTTP/JSON, human-readable; gRPC — a binary protocol (Protobuf), faster, typed
REST — a binary Protobuf protocol with streaming; gRPC — only text JSON over HTTP/1.1
REST and gRPC are the same, both have no contracts and always use only a JSON body
gRPC is only for browser forms, REST is only for internal service-to-service calls
items.e: REST: text-based, easy to debug, wide support. gRPC: more efficient (binary), streaming, code generation, typing via Protobuf.

o: A query language where the client specifies exactly which fields it needs — avoids over/under-fetching
items.e: GraphQL: one endpoint, the client requests only the needed fields. Solves over-fetching (extra data) and under-fetching (multiple requests).

items.q: What is idempotency in an API?
o: Repeated requests with the same ID give the same result without side effects
items.e: Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE — safe to repeat. POST is not idempotent. An Idempotency-Key makes POST safe.

o: Limiting the number of requests from a client per unit of time
items.e: Rate limiting: 100 req/min per user. Algorithms: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window, Sliding Window. 429 Too Many Requests.

items.q: What is the circuit breaker pattern?
o: Automatically stops requests to an unavailable service to avoid cascading failures
items.e: Circuit Breaker: Closed (normal) → Open (service down, fail fast) → Half-Open (probing). Hystrix, Resilience4j.

items.q: What is retry with exponential backoff?
o: Retries with an exponentially growing delay between them
items.e: Exponential backoff: 1s → 2s → 4s → 8s + jitter. Avoids the thundering herd problem during mass failures.

o: The system reaches a consistent state over time, without guaranteeing immediate consistency
items.e: Eventual consistency: after a write, replicas may temporarily differ. Fine for DNS, an Amazon cart. Not for banks.

o: A distributed system can only guarantee 2 of 3: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance
Any database always guarantees Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance at once
A REST API rule requiring cacheable, atomic and persistent responses for every endpoint
A set of microservice properties: containerization, authentication and performance under load
items.e: CAP: during a network partition you must choose between C (all nodes see the same data) and A (the system responds).

o: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — transaction guarantees in relational DBs
items.e: ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid data), Isolation (independent transactions), Durability (persisted after commit).

o: A data structure that speeds up lookups at the cost of extra space and slower writes
A data constraint that guarantees row uniqueness and replaces all foreign keys
A separate table schema for storing migration history and rollback scripts in production
A SELECT result cache that automatically invalidates after every transaction commit
items.e: An index (B-tree, Hash): faster SELECTs, but slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Excessive indexes hurt write performance.

items.q: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL?
o: SQL — relational, ACID, schema; NoSQL — various models, more flexible, horizontal scaling
NoSQL is only for big data
items.e: SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL): joins, transactions. NoSQL: MongoDB (document), Redis (key-value), Cassandra (wide-column), Neo4j (graph).

o: Horizontal partitioning — splitting data across several DB servers by a key
items.e: Sharding: user_id % 4 → 4 different servers. Scales writes. Complicates cross-shard joins and transactions.

o: Copying data between Primary and Replica nodes for read scaling and fault tolerance
items.e: Master-Replica: writes → Primary, reads → Replicas. Failover when the Primary fails. Async replication → eventual consistency.

items.q: What is caching and what is it for?
o: Storing frequently requested data in fast storage (RAM) to reduce DB load
Saving all logs in slow storage for auditing and incident search
A request queue between services guaranteeing processing order and delivery retries
A full database copy for writes that is always synchronous and replaces the primary
items.e: Cache (Redis, Memcached): microsecond latency instead of milliseconds. Cache-aside, Write-through, Write-behind — strategies.

o: Removing or updating stale data in the cache
items.e: "There are only two hard things in CS: cache invalidation and naming things." TTL, event-driven invalidation — approaches.

o: Asynchronous communication between services via an intermediate buffer
items.e: Message Queue (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS): producer → queue → consumer. Decoupling, async, buffering during load spikes.

items.q: What is the difference between RabbitMQ and Kafka?
o: RabbitMQ — a traditional queue (push, deletes after consumption); Kafka — an event log (pull, retains, replay)
RabbitMQ — an immutable event log with replay; Kafka — a queue that deletes messages right after ack
RabbitMQ and Kafka share the same model, only the client connection protocol differs
Kafka is only for RPC calls, RabbitMQ is only for storing event history
items.e: RabbitMQ: message broker, routing, Dead Letter Queue. Kafka: event streaming, high throughput, retention, consumer groups, replay.

o: A publisher emits events, subscribers receive them with no direct link between them
items.e: Pub/Sub: the publisher doesn't know the subscribers. Topic-based routing. Google Pub/Sub, Kafka, SNS — examples.

o: An infrastructure layer managing service-to-service communication (mTLS, tracing, retries)
A single gateway for external clients replacing all internal service-to-service calls
An L4 load balancer that only distributes TCP traffic between identical instances
A library in every service where retry, tracing and TLS logic is implemented manually
items.e: A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd): a sidecar proxy per service. Handles mTLS, circuit breaking, retries, observability with no code changes.

o: Packaging an app with its dependencies into an isolated container for a reproducible environment
items.e: Docker containers: isolated, lighter than VMs, identical on dev/staging/prod. Dockerfile → Image → Container.

o: A container orchestrator — automates deployment, scaling and container management
items.e: K8s: Pod (container), Deployment (desired state), Service (networking), Ingress (external traffic). Auto-scaling, self-healing.

items.q: What is a health check in microservices?
o: A /health endpoint returning the service state for the load balancer and orchestrator
items.e: /health: liveness (is the process alive) and readiness (is it ready for traffic). K8s and LBs exclude unhealthy instances.

o: Tracking a request across all microservices using a trace ID and spans
items.e: Distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry): a trace_id across all services → see where the latency and failures are.

o: The ability to understand a system's internal state via Logs, Metrics, Traces
items.e: The 3 pillars of observability: Logs (what happened), Metrics (numbers), Traces (request path). Prometheus, Grafana, ELK Stack, Jaeger.

o: SLI — a metric (uptime 99.9%); SLO — a target; SLA — a contract with penalties
items.e: SLI: a measured metric (error rate). SLO: a target (error rate < 0.1%). SLA: a customer contract with consequences for SLO violations.

o: Deliberately injecting failures into production to verify system resilience
items.e: Chaos Engineering (Netflix Chaos Monkey): kill services, inject latency, terminate nodes — check the system degrades gracefully.

o: Two identical environments (blue/green) — traffic switches instantly with zero downtime
items.e: Blue-Green: production = blue, new version = green. The LB switches traffic instantly. Rollback = switch back.

o: A gradual rollout of the new version — first 1-5% of traffic, then more
items.e: Canary: 5% of traffic to the new version → monitoring → 25% → 100%. Or rollback. Less risky than a full deploy.

o: Enabling/disabling functionality without a deploy via configuration
items.e: Feature flags: if (featureEnabled("new-ui")) { ... } — deploy the code, enable later. LaunchDarkly, Unleash.

o: Testing that the API producer and consumer follow an agreed contract
items.e: Contract testing (Pact): the consumer generates expectations → the provider verifies them. Replaces heavy E2E tests for microservices.

items.q: What is Pact in the context of testing?
o: A framework for consumer-driven contract testing between microservices
items.e: Pact: the consumer writes a test with expectations → a pact file → the provider verifies. A broker stores contracts. Detects breaking changes.

items.q: What specifically should be tested in microservices?
o: Contract testing, service isolation, network failures, eventual consistency, idempotency
Only unit tests inside each service without contracts, network or dependencies
Only E2E tests through the UI since they fully cover service-to-service integrations
Only single-service performance without retry, timeouts, data consistency or failure modes
items.e: Microservices: contracts between services, behavior when dependencies are down, retry logic, idempotency, eventual consistency state.

o: Managed DB schema changes via versioned scripts (Flyway, Liquibase)
items.e: Flyway/Liquibase: V1__create_users.sql, V2__add_email_index.sql — versioned migrations. Applied automatically on startup.

o: A set of pre-established DB connections for reuse
items.e: Connection pool (HikariCP): DB connections are expensive. The pool keeps N ready connections. maxPoolSize, connectionTimeout — key settings.

items.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
o: 1 query for the list + N queries per item — instead of a single JOIN query
items.e: N+1: getUsers() → 1 query, then per user → getOrders() → N queries. Fix: eager loading (JOIN FETCH), batch loading.

o: Command Query Responsibility Segregation — separate models for reads and writes
items.e: CQRS: Write model (Commands) → Event Store → Read model (Queries/Views). Optimize reads and writes independently.

o: Storing all state changes as a sequence of events instead of the current state
items.e: Event Sourcing: AccountCreated → MoneyDeposited → MoneyWithdrawn — the full history. Replaying events = rebuilding state.

items.q: What should be tested in event-driven systems?
o: Event publishing and consumption, structure, ordering, handler idempotency, replay
items.e: Event-driven testing: event contracts (schema), publish happened, consumer processed, idempotency, ordering guarantees.

items.q: What is API versioning and why?
o: Versioning an API for backward compatibility on breaking changes
items.e: API versioning: /v1/users → /v2/users or an Accept header. Lets the API evolve without breaking old clients.

o: The system keeps partially working when some components fail
items.e: Graceful degradation: the payment service is down → show a message and still allow browsing the catalog.

o: Resource isolation between components — one failure doesn't consume the others' resources
items.e: Bulkhead: separate thread pools per service. If service A hangs — it doesn't block service B. Resilience4j.

items.q: What is a timeout in distributed systems?
o: The maximum time to wait for a response from a dependency
items.e: Connection timeout, read timeout — different levels. No timeout = infinite waiting = the whole system hangs.

o: Distributed transactions via a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure
A central ACID transaction locking all services until the business process completes
A caching pattern for service responses with TTL and automatic invalidation
A retry mechanism without compensations that just repeats the failed request until success
items.e: Saga: Order → Reserve Inventory → Charge Payment → Ship. On failure — compensating transactions. Choreography or Orchestration.

o: A unique request key that makes POST safe to repeat without duplication
items.e: Idempotency-Key: POST /payments + a UUID — the server caches the result. A repeat request → the same response, no reprocessing.

o: A centralized repository for message schemas (Avro, Protobuf) in Kafka
items.e: Confluent Schema Registry: the producer registers the schema, the consumer validates. Backward/forward compatibility is checked automatically.

o: A mechanism for dynamically finding service addresses without hardcoding
items.e: Service discovery (Consul, Eureka, K8s DNS): services register themselves → clients resolve addresses dynamically.

items.q: What is security testing in the context of APIs?
o: OWASP Top 10: injection, broken auth, IDOR, rate limiting, excessive data exposure
items.e: API security: SQL injection, IDOR, broken auth, missing rate limiting, verbose error messages, JWT validation.

o: A list of the 10 most critical web application security risks
items.e: OWASP Top 10: Injection, Broken Auth, Sensitive Data Exposure, XXE, Broken Access Control, XSS, Insecure Deserialization etc.

o: Injecting SQL code through input data to manipulate the DB
items.e: SQL injection: " OR 1=1-- in a login field. Protection: prepared statements, ORMs, parameterized queries.

o: Injecting malicious JS into a page that runs in the victim's browser
items.e: XSS: <script>stealCookies()</script> in a comment. Stored, Reflected, DOM-based. Protection: escaping, CSP, sanitization.

o: Forcing the victim's browser to make a request on their behalf to another site
items.e: CSRF: a malicious site → a form POST to bank.com. Protection: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, Origin/Referer checks.

items.q: What should QA test in a microservice architecture?
o: Integration between services, contract testing, failure scenarios, data consistency, tracing
items.e: QA for microservices: contract testing, consumer-driven contracts, chaos testing, distributed tracing, cross-service data consistency.

o: A machine-readable REST API specification — the single source of truth for the API structure
items.e: OpenAPI (Swagger): auto-generated SDKs, mock servers, test cases. Contract testing from the spec. Always-current documentation.
